clue.text: Stints work that is theatrical on board

indicators.note: something carried on board a ship sits within the vessel, so these letters go inside the ship's abbreviation

blocks.note: camp means exaggerated and showy, like a stage performance
SS is a steamship, so being on board means sitting inside those letters

explanation.surface: Someone skimps on a job that turns out to be a showy bit of play-acting on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'on board' a ship is a crossword convention for sitting between S and S.
explanation.definitionFit: To scamp a job is an old verb for doing it carelessly or skimping, so scamps means stints on the labour.

clue.text: American plane in which Mr O'Casey crashed

indicators.note: a crashed vehicle is wrecked and jumbled, so the letters of the name are scrambled

blocks.note: the playwright's name, letters taken as written

explanation.surface: The Irish playwright Sean O'Casey is caught in an air crash on an American aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' looks like an aeroplane, which suits 'crashed'; it is the tree. In America the plane tree is called a sycamore.
explanation.definitionFit: The American sycamore belongs to the plane genus Platanus, and Americans call plane trees sycamores.

clue.text: Hands brought together in concord, say

definitions.text: Hands brought together in concord, say

blocks.note: surface reading: people joining hands in harmony and agreement
setter's reading: Concorde the supersonic airliner, with its hands being the people who staff it in flight

explanation.surface: People clasp hands in a gesture of harmony and agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: Hands are workers or crew members, and 'say' marks Concord as an example of an aircraft rather than a state of peace.
explanation.definitionFit: The staff who fly and serve aboard an aircraft such as Concorde are its flight team, the hands working in the air.

clue.text: Dives with power?

blocks.note: surface reading: plunges downward forcefully
setter's reading: Dives is the rich man of the Bible parable, so a wealthy person who also holds power

explanation.surface: Someone plunges into the water with great force.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives, from the Latin for rich, is the traditional name of the wealthy man in the parable of Lazarus; add power and you have rule by the rich.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocrat is a person whose wealth gives them political influence, a rich man holding power.

clue.text: This goose is one very difficult to get rid of

definitions.text: one very difficult to get rid of

blocks.note: first meaning: a black and white Arctic goose species

blocks.clueFragment: one very difficult to get rid of
blocks.note: second meaning: a hanger-on who clings like the shellfish on a ship's hull

explanation.surface: A particular goose has a habit of sticking around and refusing to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: The barnacle goose is a named species, and the clinging shellfish gives the figurative sense of a persistent hanger-on.

clue.text: Something to stimulate adeptness in art movement

indicators.note: movement suggests the letters shift position and are moved into a fresh order

blocks.note: letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An artistic movement is something that sparks skill in its painters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Art movement' reads as one phrase, like Cubism; 'movement' is in fact telling you to rearrange the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug that lifts mood counters depression, so it is a stimulant to the spirits in a loose sense.

clue.text: Downtown reported fresh lines

blocks.note: fresh means new
RY is the abbreviation for railway, and railway lines are its track

explanation.surface: A city centre is said to have new railway lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Downtown' is not a city centre but a town in County Down, Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Newry is a city on the border of County Down and County Armagh in Northern Ireland, so it is a town of Down.

clue.text: Careful opening bids for treasure-chests

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its very beginning, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: the start of the word careful
bids at an auction are offers

explanation.surface: Cautious opening bids at an auction for some old treasure chests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Careful opening bids' reads as cautious first offers; 'opening' actually takes just the first letter of 'Careful'.
explanation.definitionFit: Coffers are strong boxes for keeping money or valuables, the literal chests a treasury takes its name from.

clue.text: Wearily chiming in such a spooky way

indicators.note: words that chime ring alike, so the answer is found by sound, rhyming with the word before

blocks.note: said out loud without its opening W, the word for tired behaviour chimes exactly with the spooky adverb

explanation.surface: Bells ring slowly and tiredly, giving a ghostly atmosphere.
explanation.walkthrough: Chiming here means rhyming: the answer and 'wearily' sound alike apart from the first consonant.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie means strange and frightening, so doing something eerily is behaving in a spooky, unsettling manner.

clue.text: First of the high  summers in Cambridge?

definitions.text: First of the high  summers in Cambridge?

blocks.note: surface reading: the first of the warm summer seasons
setter's reading: summers are people who do sums, and the first of them at Cambridge is the top mathematics student

explanation.surface: The start of a long hot summer season in a university town.
explanation.walkthrough: Summers here are people who sum. At Cambridge the student placed top in the mathematics Tripos was traditionally given this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The title was given to the student who came first among Cambridge mathematics graduates, the best of its number-crunchers.

clue.text: French hornpipe not extremely bulky

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: split as French horn plus pipe: cor is French for horn, and to pule, like to pipe, is to cry thinly
only the two end letters of the word are used

explanation.surface: A French sailor's hornpipe dance that is not too heavy-footed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hornpipe' must be split into horn and pipe. To pule is an old word for to whimper, as to pipe is to cry in a high voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpulent describes a person who is fat and heavily built, which is a close synonym of bulky.

clue.text: Biscuit eaten on a Sunday, say?

definitions.text: Biscuit eaten on a Sunday, say?

blocks.note: surface reading: a treat nibbled at the weekend
setter's reading: the thin bread taken at Holy Communion in church services

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys a biscuit as a weekend treat.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'say' points to a Sunday church service, where Communion is received as a thin disc of unleavened bread.
explanation.definitionFit: A wafer is both a thin crisp biscuit and the consecrated disc given at the Eucharist in church.

clue.text: First signalman over the pond

blocks.note: surface reading: a senior railway signal operator
setter's reading: the inventor who sent the first radio signal across the Atlantic, the pond

explanation.surface: The head railway signal operator stationed beside a pond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The pond' is a jokey name for the Atlantic Ocean; the Italian radio pioneer sent the first transatlantic wireless signal in 1901.
explanation.definitionFit: Guglielmo Marconi transmitted the first radio message from Cornwall to Newfoundland, signalling across the ocean before anyone else.

clue.text: Boring hole in a battery

blocks.note: dull, uninteresting writing or talk is called dry
a hole is a cramped, dingy room, as is a prison cell

explanation.surface: Drilling a hole into a battery of guns or cells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring hole' reads as drilling; 'Boring' is the adjective dull.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry cell is the common torch battery, where the electrolyte is a paste rather than liquid.

clue.text: He uses the sweep stroke, perhaps

definitions.text: He uses the sweep stroke, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: a swimmer, painter or golfer making a broad sweeping movement
setter's reading: in sweep boats each oarsman pulls one long oar, and stroke is the seat setting the pace

explanation.surface: A man makes a broad, sweeping movement in some sport or craft.
explanation.walkthrough: A sweep is a long oar, and stroke is the crew member nearest the stern who sets the rhythm for the boat.
explanation.definitionFit: An oarsman propels a boat with oars, and a sweep oarsman may sit at stroke, the pace-setting position.

clue.text: Peace around America, ham, hammered into shape

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the word for peace is wrapped about the country's abbreviation

blocks.note: repose is a state of peace and rest
US is the standard abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: A peace settlement involving America is forged with heavy blows.
explanation.walkthrough: The rest wraps around US, sitting after its fourth letter. The word 'ham' adds nothing to the wordplay and looks like a stray from the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Repoussé metalwork is formed by hammering a sheet from the reverse side to raise a relief design.

clue.text: Powered by water, landed short of the runway

blocks.note: first meaning: a mill wheel turned by water flowing beneath it
second meaning: an aircraft that touched down before reaching the tarmac

explanation.surface: A water-powered aircraft came down before reaching the airstrip.
explanation.definitionFit: An undershot wheel is driven by water passing under it, and to undershoot is to fall short of a target when landing.

clue.text: Cardinal with almost sensual nose

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word for sensual loses its final letter

blocks.note: gross means coarsely sensual or carnal
beak is slang for a nose

explanation.surface: A church cardinal with a rather fleshy, sensuous nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' suggests a Catholic prelate; it is the North American songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: The cardinal is a thick-billed songbird of the finch family, and such birds are known by this name.

clue.text: Job vacant with carriage provided

blocks.note: a post is a position of employment
a vacant seat or room is free

explanation.surface: A job advertisement for an unfilled post that comes with a company car.
explanation.walkthrough: Carriage here means the cost of delivery, not a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods sent without a postage charge to the buyer have delivery costs covered by the seller.

clue.text: I, Ronald, travelling first for example

indicators.note: letters that are travelling move about and do not stay in their original order

blocks.note: letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Ronald says he went on his journeys first class, as it were.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinal numbers such as first, second and third show position in a sequence rather than quantity.

clue.text: Alternative to last month's scenery

blocks.note: Dec is the abbreviation for December, the last month of the year
or is the word that introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Something offered instead of last month's stage backdrop.
explanation.definitionFit: Décor can mean the scenery and set dressing of a stage production, as well as interior decoration.

clue.text: Hint about one shortcoming in the cooking

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for hint goes round the other pieces

blocks.note: a cue is a prompt or hint
Roman numeral one
a sin is a moral failing

explanation.surface: A suggestion that one flaw lies in the way the food was prepared.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuisine is a style or method of preparing food, the cooking characteristic of a place or restaurant.

clue.text: Frank to reduce Shaw's titled lady

indicators.note: to reduce something is to make it shorter, so the play's title loses its last letter

blocks.note: Candida is the title character of a George Bernard Shaw play

explanation.surface: A man named Frank sets out to cut down a Shavian heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name; it is the adjective meaning open and honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Candid and frank both describe speech that is honest and straightforward, saying plainly what one thinks.

clue.text: Hot-dog in the hearth

blocks.note: surface reading: a sausage in a bun, or a pet warming itself
setter's reading: a firedog, the metal support that holds logs in a fireplace and gets hot

explanation.surface: A dog lies by the fireplace getting too warm.
explanation.walkthrough: A firedog is a metal stand that supports burning logs; being in the fire, it is literally a hot dog.
explanation.definitionFit: An andiron is one of a pair of metal log supports in a fireplace, also called a firedog.

clue.text: Send watch back

indicators.note: back tells you to read the word for watch from its end to its start

blocks.note: a watch is a timer

explanation.surface: An instruction to return a wristwatch to the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit is to send or transmit, especially money, or to refer a matter to an authority.

clue.text: Sounds in need

blocks.note: first meaning: narrow channels of sea, as a sound is
second meaning: hardship, as in being in dire financial trouble

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' looks like noises or a verb; it is the geographical sense of a sea channel. 'In need' matches being in straits.
explanation.definitionFit: Straits are narrow sea passages, also called sounds, and the plural also means a position of difficulty or distress.

clue.text: Unearthed replacement material here

indicators.note: a replacement puts letters in new places, so the word for unearthed is reordered

blocks.note: something dug out of the ground has been mined

explanation.surface: Something dug up turns out to be a substitute fabric found on the spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is a hard-wearing twill cotton fabric used for jeans, so it is a type of cloth.

clue.text: The hour of the ploughman of course

definitions.text: The hour of the ploughman of course

blocks.note: surface reading: the time a farm labourer gets up to work the fields
setter's reading: a ploughman's is a British pub meal of bread, cheese and pickle, eaten at midday

explanation.surface: Naturally, there is a set time for the farmer to go out ploughing.
explanation.walkthrough: A ploughman's is a British pub dish of bread, cheese and pickle, and 'of course' suggests a meal course.
explanation.definitionFit: The ploughman's is a meal eaten in the middle of the day, so its hour is the midday meal break.

clue.text: New diary left to get behind-hand

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so these letters are formed into a different arrangement

blocks.note: letters taken as written
L is the standard abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fresh appointment diary is abandoned, so its owner falls behind schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Dilatory means slow or tending to delay, which is the old sense of being behind-hand with one's tasks.

clue.text: How some run at Lord's, having no cover

definitions.text: How some run at Lord's, having no cover

blocks.clueFragment: How some run at Lord's, having no cover
blocks.note: surface reading: batsmen taking runs at the cricket ground with no fielder in the cover position

blocks.clueFragment: run at Lord's, having no cover
blocks.note: setter's reading: dashing naked across the pitch in front of the crowd

explanation.surface: Batsmen scamper runs at a famous cricket ground because no fielder is placed at cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground, and cover is a fielding position; here 'no cover' means no clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To streak is to run naked through a public place, a stunt famously performed at sporting events.
